questions.question: What does @functools.wraps do on a wrapper function?
options: It runs the wrapped function immediately
It copies the wrapped function's metadata — name, docstring and signature — onto the wrapper
It caches the result of the wrapped function
questions.explanation: functools.wraps copies __name__, __doc__, __wrapped__ and the signature from the wrapped function onto the wrapper, so introspection keeps working. It does not run, cache or lock anything.

questions.question: Given @outer stacked above @inner on a function, which wrapper runs first when the function is called?
options: outer, because it is written first
inner, because it is applied first and sits closest to the function
Both run at the same time
Neither — only the topmost decorator applies
questions.explanation: Decorators are applied bottom-up: the decorator closest to the function is applied first, so inner wraps the function and outer wraps inner. At call time the call enters outer's wrapper first and reaches inner's wrapper last.

questions.question: Which of these belong in a decorator wrapper's signature? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A wrapper must accept whatever the wrapped function accepts, so it takes *args and **kwargs and forwards them. A fixed signature like wrapper(n: int) breaks the moment the caller passes something else.

questions.question: A decorator is applied to the function every time the function is called.
questions.explanation: False. Decoration happens once, at definition time — @decorator is shorthand for name = decorator(name). The wrapper is what runs on every call.
